parsed.elsewhere_quote: a move with $g=\gcd(m,n)$ sends $P\mapsto P/g$; if $g\ge2$ the product at least halves, if $g=1$ the product is kept but $z$ increases by $1$ (and $z$ never decreases), so there are at most $\lfloor\log_2 P_0\rfloor + 2026$ moves. Moreover no move can produce two $1$'s, so some entry $>1$ always survives, and the terminal position has **exactly one** entry $M>1$.
parsed.explanation: The objection correctly identifies a local logical gap: before finiteness is known, an infinite play has no $P_{\mathrm{final}}$. The inequality must instead be applied after each finite prefix containing $t$ Type A moves. However, the “Current best” section independently gives the bounded-move argument without invoking a final product and also establishes exactly one survivor. Thus L1.1 is established elsewhere as written; replacing the quoted sentence by the finite-prefix formulation repairs the full-proof passage.
